Simulate respondents with a language model (experimental)

Source: R/ai-synthetic.R
simulate_llm_respondents.Rd

Experimental. simulate_llm_respondents() asks a language model to answer multiple-choice items as each of a list of described respondents ("personas") would, and scores the answers. Some researchers use such "synthetic respondents" or "silicon samples" to try out items before a field test. Whether their answers behave like real test takers' answers is an open question, and the evidence so far is mixed: Language models tend to find items too easy, to answer more consistently than people, and to act out stereotypes of the groups they are asked to play. Treat the results as a hypothesis about the items, never as a replacement for responses from real people, and always check them against real data with compare_synthetic().

Usage

simulate_llm_respondents(
  items,
  personas,
  stem = "stem",
  options = NULL,
  key = "key",
  id = "id",
  provider = NULL,
  model = NULL
)

Arguments

items

a data frame with one row per multiple-choice item, such as itemtext.

personas

the respondents to simulate: A character vector of descriptions ("A Grade 7 student who struggles with fractions"), or a data frame with a persona column and any other columns that describe them (kept in the output).

stem, key, id

names of the columns with the stem, the letter of the keyed option and the item id.

options

names of the option columns; by default the columns A to E that exist.

provider, model

the language model, as in mv_ask(). By default the one chosen with mv_ask_setup(), or the recordings when mv_llm_replay() is on.

Value

An object of class mv_synthetic: A list with responses (a data frame of scored responses, 1 correct, 0 wrong and NA when the model gave no usable answer, one row per persona and one column per item), answers (the option letters chosen), personas (a tibble with an id and the persona columns), items (item ids and keys), provider and model. It has print() and compare_synthetic() methods; pass $responses to mirt::mirt() like any response data.

Details

Each persona is one request, which lists every item. The model is asked to answer as the persona would, mistakes included, and to give one option letter per item.

The function and its output may change in later versions of mirtverse.

References

Argyle, L. P., Busby, E. C., Fulda, N., Gubler, J. R., Rytting, C., & Wingate, D. (2023). Out of one, many: Using language models to simulate human samples. Political Analysis, 31(3), 337-351.

See also

compare_synthetic(); the book's chapter on large language models; the AI Hub.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("ellmer", quietly = TRUE)) {
  old <- mv_llm_replay()        # answer from the recordings that come with mirtverse
  items <- itemtext[endsWith(itemtext$id, "-01"), ]
  personas <- c(
    "A Grade 7 student who struggles with mathematics.",
    "A Grade 7 student who struggles with mathematics and is still learning English.",
    "A Grade 7 student who finds fractions and decimals hard but tries every question.",
    "A Grade 7 student who often rushes and makes careless mistakes.",
    "A Grade 7 student who is about average in mathematics.",
    "A Grade 7 student who is about average in mathematics and is still learning English.",
    "A Grade 7 student with average marks who is anxious on tests.",
    "A Grade 7 student who is about average in mathematics and likes word problems.",
    "A Grade 7 student who is strong in mathematics.",
    "A Grade 7 student who is strong in mathematics and is still learning English.",
    "A Grade 7 student in an enriched mathematics program.",
    "A Grade 7 student who is strong in mathematics but reads slowly.")
  syn <- simulate_llm_respondents(items, personas)
  syn
  compare_synthetic(syn, stats::setNames(items$p_field, items$id))
  options(old)
}
#> Language model calls now answer from examples.json (23 recorded requests).
# }
